clue.text: Fellow Charlie most pleased shedding stone

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

indicators.note: to shed something is to cast it off, so the named weight comes away from the word

parts.note: the superlative of happy
st is the abbreviation for stone, the British unit of weight

explanation.surface: A man called Charlie, delighted at having lost a stone in weight.
explanation.walkthrough: HAPPIEST loses ST to leave HAPPIE, and C goes in front. A stone is a British weight of fourteen pounds, abbreviated st.
explanation.definitionFit: Chappie is an informal, rather old-fashioned British word for a man or chap, so it serves as a synonym for fellow.

clue.text: Revolutionary glum in camp, saying nothing

indicators.note: a revolution overturns the existing order, so these letters are turned over into a fresh arrangement

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A gloomy revolutionary sits silently in a guerrilla camp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' reads as a noun for a rebel in the camp, but it is only the signal to rearrange the ten letters that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: To clam up is an idiom for falling silent or refusing to talk, like a clam shutting its shell.

clue.text: Change result after graduate getting upset

indicators.note: one piece is placed following the other in the finished word
in a down clue, to upset something is to tip it over so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts, a graduate degree
an end is an outcome or result

explanation.surface: A graduate is upset after the outcome of an exam gets changed.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue an upset word reads from the bottom up, so the degree is written backwards before the outcome is added beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend a text or law is to alter or revise it, so the verb is a direct synonym for change.

clue.text: One demonstrates for person making examination

parts.note: pro means for or in favour of
someone who tests or examines

explanation.surface: Someone demonstrates something on behalf of an examiner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demonstrates for' looks like a teacher showing a method, but 'for' splits off as PRO. The definition is a compressed 'one who demonstrates'.
explanation.definitionFit: A protester takes part in public demonstrations against something, so one who demonstrates describes the role exactly.

clue.text: This writer's turned on ally, topped in malevolent way

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another comes above it
something turned round faces the opposite way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: the setter speaking of themselves: I have, contracted to I've

indicators.note: to top something is to cut off its head, so the first letter is lost

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The setter confesses to having betrayed a friend in a spiteful manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer's' stands for I'VE (I have), which turned gives EVI; ALLY loses its top letter to leave LLY beneath.
explanation.definitionFit: Evil means wicked or malicious, and the adverb describes acting with ill will, which is what malevolent means.

clue.text: Pressure to behave to gain agreement

parts.note: P is the symbol for pressure in physics
to act is to behave in a certain way

explanation.surface: Someone is pressured into behaving well so a deal can be reached.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the standard abbreviation for pressure, and ACT follows it.
explanation.definitionFit: A pact is a formal treaty or deal between parties, so it is a straightforward synonym for an agreement.

clue.text: Quietly greeting Greek character

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction to play quietly
a casual greeting

explanation.surface: A soft-spoken hello to a man from Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character' suggests a person from Greece, but here it means a letter of the Greek alphabet.
explanation.definitionFit: Phi is the twenty-first letter of the Greek alphabet, and character is a standard term for a written letter.

clue.text: Son wrapped in jacket on exposed walk along the shore

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece sitting on another comes above it
something wrapped in a garment is enclosed by it, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: a coat is a jacket
S is the abbreviation for son

indicators.note: exposed means stripped of its covering, so the outside letters are peeled away

parts.note: the inner letters of the word, its first and last removed

explanation.surface: A boy bundled up in his coat strolls on a windswept beach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exposed walk' paints a windy seafront, but 'exposed' means the word is stripped of its outer letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Coastal is the adjective for things situated by the sea, describing what lies by or along the shore.

clue.text: Alcoholic drink valet removed from case

indicators.note: taking something out of its case strips away the outer shell, keeping only the inside

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A valet unpacks a bottle of booze from a suitcase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' suggests luggage a valet would handle, but it means the outer letters of the word, which are discarded.
explanation.definitionFit: Ale is a type of beer brewed with top-fermenting yeast, so it is an example of an alcoholic drink.

clue.text: First love, a girl in Barking

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, shaped like the letter O

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, and crazy letters are jumbled into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone recalls their first love, a girl who lived in Barking.
explanation.walkthrough: Barking is a district of East London, which is what the surface wants; in British slang barking (barking mad) means crazy, the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Original can mean earliest or initial, as in the original owner, so it is a synonym for first.

clue.text: Disorganised fight where no one's charged?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a chaotic brawl in which anyone may join
second meaning, read literally: an event costing nothing for anyone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charged' sounds like a police matter after a brawl, but it means asked to pay; the question mark flags the literal reading of the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A free-for-all is an idiom for an unruly brawl or scramble, and taken word by word it means no cost to anybody.

clue.text: Insect regularly bit dogs in Middle East

indicators.note: placed inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: ME is the abbreviation for the Middle East

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: Some biting insect keeps nipping dogs somewhere in the Middle East.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bit dogs' sounds like an attack, but 'regularly' asks for every other letter across both words, ignoring the space.
explanation.definitionFit: A midge is a tiny two-winged fly, often a biting one, so it is a specific example of an insect.

clue.text: Rotating egret's boldly catching shellfish

indicators.note: turning right round makes the letters run in the opposite direction
to catch is to hold, so the words hold the answer within them

parts.note: the letters spanning the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: A wheeling egret swoops confidently to snatch a crab or crayfish from the water.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run backwards inside the two words, across the apostrophe-s and the start of boldly.
explanation.definitionFit: A lobster is a large marine crustacean with claws, and crustaceans eaten as seafood count as shellfish.

clue.text: They secure footwear, and loose cables too

indicators.note: loose things are not held in place, so these letters are free to rearrange

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Things that hold shoes on, plus some stray wires as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too' looks like padding, but its letters are needed to complete the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Bootlaces are the cords threaded through eyelets that tie boots tightly to the feet, fastening the footwear in place.

clue.text: Figure in Spielberg film set in New York

indicators.note: to be set in a place is to be located inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: NY is the abbreviation for New York
taken as written
E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, the 1982 Spielberg film

explanation.surface: A character appears in a Spielberg movie whose action takes place in New York.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' suggests a person on screen, but it means a number. 'In' is kept as letters rather than read as a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ninety is a number, and figure is a common word for a numeral or numerical amount.

clue.text: Comparatively horrible when drawn into new row

indicators.note: something drawn into a space is pulled inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
a tier is a row, as of seats

explanation.surface: Things get even more unpleasant when someone is pulled into a fresh quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' in the surface rhymes with cow and means a quarrel, but it is the other sense, a line of seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Nastier is the comparative form of nasty, meaning more unpleasant, which is what comparatively horrible expresses.

clue.text: Footballer's advanced position after start

indicators.note: placed following in sequence, so the earlier piece leads

parts.note: a go is a start or attempt, as in 'have a go'
A is the abbreviation for advanced, as in A-level
the lie of something is its position, as in the lie of the land

explanation.surface: A footballer pushes into an attacking position after kick-off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advanced position' reads as a forward's place on the pitch, ironic since the answer is the player furthest back.
explanation.definitionFit: A goalie is the goalkeeper, the specific player on a football team who guards the net.

clue.text: Rejected clues editor was hostile towards

indicators.note: a rejected thing is thrown back, so its letters are sent the other way

parts.note: tips are hints or clues
ed is the abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: A crossword editor turned down a setter's clues out of animosity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rejected clues' sounds like an editor's verdict, but 'rejected' sends the synonym for clues backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To spite someone is to deliberately hurt or annoy them out of malice, an act of open ill will.

clue.text: Slacken binding of some nun's trappings

indicators.note: only a part of the following words is wanted, carried inside them

parts.note: letters running from the second of the first word into the second word

explanation.surface: Loosening the ties of a nun's habit and accessories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Binding' seems to belong with the nun's trappings, but it is part of the definition; the answer straddles the apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: To unstrap is to undo a strap or buckle, loosening a fastening that holds something tight.

clue.text: Drunk loses first game of chance

indicators.note: losing the opening letter means the word is beheaded

parts.note: blotto is slang for very drunk

explanation.surface: A drunk gambler loses the first round of a betting game.
explanation.walkthrough: BLOTTO, British slang for extremely drunk, drops its B.
explanation.definitionFit: Lotto is a lottery or a bingo-like game where numbers are drawn at random, so winning depends entirely on luck.

clue.text: Sound of disapproval following cheers is not acceptable

indicators.note: coming after in sequence, so the earlier piece leads

parts.note: ta is British slang for thanks, as is cheers
a jeer from a crowd

explanation.surface: A crowd jeers after people raise a toast, signalling the behaviour is out of line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cheers' suggests a toast or applause, but in Britain both cheers and ta are casual ways of saying thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Something taboo is prohibited by social custom, forbidden or beyond the pale, so it is not acceptable.

clue.text: Mammoth — caging it is complicated

indicators.note: something complicated is tangled and involved, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Keeping a woolly mammoth in an enclosure is a tricky business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mammoth' reads as the prehistoric beast being caged, but it is the adjective meaning huge.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective, mammoth means enormous or huge, and gigantic is a direct synonym for something of vast size.

clue.text: Affirmative vote first person read aloud

indicators.note: reading out loud means only the sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: I is the first-person pronoun

explanation.surface: A voter says yes, and the first name on the list is called out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'First person' suggests the person at the front, but it is the grammatical first person, the pronoun I.
explanation.definitionFit: Aye is the word for yes used in parliamentary and committee voting, as in 'the ayes have it'.

clue.text: Snake starts to be overly aggressive

indicators.note: the starts of words are their opening letters, which are kept

parts.note: the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: A snake begins to act with too much hostility.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts' reads as a verb, the snake beginning to turn aggressive, but it is the noun for the initial letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A boa is a large constricting serpent of tropical America, so it is a particular kind of snake.

clue.text: Issue instructions to cut cheese

indicators.note: cutting something shortens it, so the final letter is trimmed off

parts.note: to brief someone is to give them instructions

explanation.surface: Someone is told how to slice a wedge of cheese.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut cheese' reads as one kitchen task, but 'cut' trims the last letter from BRIEF.
explanation.definitionFit: Brie is a soft, creamy French cheese with a white rind, so it is a specific variety of cheese.

clue.text: Plunder some French post office, centre of Aurillac

parts.note: des is French for 'some', used before plural nouns
PO is the abbreviation for post office

indicators.note: the centre is the middle, so only the innermost letters are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of the eight-letter town name

explanation.surface: Thieves raid a French post office in the middle of Aurillac.
explanation.walkthrough: Aurillac is a town in south-central France, which suits the surface; only its central pair of letters is used.
explanation.definitionFit: To despoil is to rob a place of its valuables by force, so it is a synonym for the verb plunder.
